analysis.one_liner: Bars most lawsuits against small-aircraft makers over planes more than 15 years old.
analysis.headline: Backed by 305 of 435 House members from both parties, the bill to cut off liability suits against aircraft manufacturers after 15 years never got a House vote; the identical Senate companion became law in 1994.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped people from suing aircraft manufacturers for crashes involving small, non-airline planes more than 15 years after the plane was first delivered, and it would have wiped out any state law that gave victims longer. Supporters said liability lawsuits and insurance costs had pushed small-plane makers toward shutting down; the price was that victims of crashes in older aircraft would have no legal claim, no matter how bad the defect.
analysis.who_benefits: Small-aircraft and aircraft-parts manufacturers gain the most: they would be immune from any lawsuit over an aircraft or component more than 15 years past its first delivery, whatever the defect, and no state could give victims longer [S3]. Pilots, flight schools, and plane buyers would benefit too if, as supporters argued, lower liability costs revive production and bring prices down — the bill's own title frames it as "revitalizing" the industry [S1].

how_it_helps.text: Bars any civil suit for death, injury, or property damage against the maker of a general aviation aircraft — or of any component, system, subassembly, or part of it — if the accident happened more than 15 years after the plane was first delivered, or 15 years after a replacement part was installed.
Overrides ('supersedes') any federal or state law that would otherwise let a victim bring such a claim after the 15-year deadline, so state courts could not apply their own longer rules.

The protection covers planes carrying fewer than 20 passengers that were not flying scheduled passenger service — the small private and business aircraft made by companies like Cessna, Piper, and Beechcraft.

analysis.who_pays: Crash victims and the families of people killed in accidents involving aircraft more than 15 years old: they lose the right to sue the manufacturer or parts maker for any defect, and the bill specifically strips away state laws that would have let them [S3]. Trial lawyers who handle these cases also lose the business [S4 context: the suits being cut off are the products-liability cases the bill targets].

drawbacks.text: Pilots, passengers, and people on the ground hurt by a defective aircraft would have no legal recourse once the plane is 15 years past first delivery — even if the defect was a hidden design or manufacturing flaw, since the bill text contains no exception for concealed defects or willful misconduct.

Many small planes stay in service for decades, so the 15-year clock would grant total immunity for most of the aircraft actually flying, cutting off compensation for the very old fleet where defect claims most often arise.
The bill preempts state tort law, so states that had deliberately given crash victims longer rights to sue would lose that authority.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The case for the bill is real, not cosmetic: liability insurance costs and lawsuits are widely credited with driving Cessna to stop making single-engine planes in 1986, and supporters argued a time limit was the only way to keep small-plane manufacturing alive in the United States (not among the provided sources, but well documented). The cost is equally real: someone killed or paralyzed by a defective 20-year-old plane gets nothing from the manufacturer, and this version of the bill offers no exception even where a maker concealed a known defect. A narrower bill — one with a fraud exception and a longer window — would have balanced these better than the 15-year cutoff in this text.

outcome.mechanism: The House never voted on the bill; it sat in two committees, held hearings, and died there, while the identical Senate companion (S. 1458) carried the proposal into law later that year.

narrative.text: Rep. Dan Glickman introduced the bill on September 15, 1993, and it was sent to both the Judiciary and Public Works and Transportation Committees the same day.
Within two weeks it reached subcommittees in both committees, and hearings were held in October 1993 and again in May 1994.
305 House members — 170 of 177 Republicans and 135 of 258 Democrats — signed on as cosponsors, an unusually large bipartisan roster for a bill limiting lawsuits.
Neither full committee ever voted the bill out, and the House never took it up; the last action, on May 17, 1994, is a note pointing to the Senate companion, S. 1458.

The proposal itself did not die: well-documented records outside this entry's source list show the identical Senate bill, S. 1458, passed that summer and was signed into law in August 1994 (Public Law 103-298), so the 15-year limit took effect even though this House bill never reached the floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: General aviation manufacturers came out ahead: they got the liability shield they sought, through the Senate companion rather than this House bill. Crash victims and their families came out on the losing side, losing claims against makers of older aircraft.

for.name: Rep. Dan Glickman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke for it on the House floor at introduction and again in March 1994.

for.name: House Subcommittee on Aviation (Public Works and Transportation) and Subcommittee on Economic and Commercial Law (Judiciary)
for.what_they_did: Held hearings on the bill in October 1993 and May 1994.

for.name: General Aviation Manufacturers Association and the small-plane makers (Cessna, Piper, Beechcraft)
for.what_they_did: Pushed for a federal time limit on liability suits, arguing lawsuit and insurance costs had shut down small-plane production.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Held hearings but never voted the bill out of committee or onto the House floor before the Congress ended.

against.name: Association of Trial Lawyers of America
against.what_they_did: Opposed time limits on products-liability suits against aircraft makers, which would eliminate crash victims' claims.

sides.party_line_note: Support split almost no party lines: the sponsor was a Kansas Democrat, 135 of 258 House Democrats and 170 of 177 House Republicans cosponsored [S4].

industries.note: The bill's entire purpose is to shield these companies (Cessna, Piper, Beechcraft and peers) from lawsuits over aircraft more than 15 years old. Their gain comes directly out of crash victims' pockets: a manufacturer's freedom from liability is a victim's lost compensation. Supporters counter that without the shield the industry might not exist at all.
The bill explicitly covers every component, system, subassembly, and part, with its own 15-year clock from installation, so parts makers get the same immunity as airframe makers.
Products-liability suits over aging small aircraft are a significant line of business for the plaintiffs' bar; the bill eliminates those claims, so their interest runs together with crash victims'.

industries.industry: General aviation operators — flight schools, charter services, aircraft owners
industries.note: Supporters argued cheaper liability would mean more planes made and sold at lower prices. But these operators also fly the aging fleet the bill insulates, and a customer or student hurt by a defect in an older plane would have no claim against the maker.
